stops.name: Buenos Aires, the house on Calle Tucumán
stops.campa: Jorge Francisco Isidoro Luis Borges is born on the fourth floor of a house on Calle Tucumán, in the small hours before dawn, the first child of Jorge Guillermo Borges, lawyer and sometime lecturer in psychology, and Leonor Acevedo Suárez, of old criollo military stock. English runs in the blood on the father's side: the grandmother, Frances Haslam, came out from Staffordshire and never lost her tongue. The house will later be torn down; the district remembers only a bronze plaque. The child inherits, unknown to anyone yet, the retina that has already begun to fail in generations before him.

stops.name: Palermo, the paternal library
stops.campa: The family's rented house in Palermo has a walled garden his mother will later call the first labyrinth, and beyond the dining room a library of English books floor to ceiling: his father's, unabridged, unlocked to the boy. Jorge Guillermo, half-blind already, cannot read them himself for many hours at a stretch and gives them instead to his son, who reads Stevenson, Twain, and Dickens, and — before he ever opens it in Spanish — an English Don Quixote, so that for years he believes chivalry a foreign invention. He will say, decades on, that no other event in his life mattered more.
stops.quote: If I were asked to name the chief event in my life, I should say my father's library.
stops.quote_source: An Autobiographical Essay, The New Yorker, 1970

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the sailing of the Sierra Nevada
stops.campa: On the third of February the whole household — Jorge Guillermo, Leonor, the two children, and the maternal grandmother — boards the German steamer Sierra Nevada, bound by way of Lisbon and Paris for Geneva, where a Swiss oculist has been named the last hope against the father's advancing blindness. No one on the dock imagines the crossing will be for good; Europe is at peace and the visit is meant to last a season. The father carries the family's darkening inheritance in his eyes; the son, not yet fifteen, carries a satchel of English books and does not yet know he carries the same darkness.

stops.name: Geneva, rue de Malagnou
stops.campa: The family takes rooms at Malagnou 17, meaning to stay a season for the father's treatment; within months the guns open on the Marne and the border to France and Germany closes around them. Geneva becomes home for five years no one planned. The boy, not yet fifteen and already reading Carlyle in English on the shores of the lake, watches the neutral city fill with refugees, spies, and the exiled of every warring nation, and begins, without noticing the hinge turning, to become a citizen of books before he is a citizen of any one country.

stops.name: Geneva, the Collège Calvin
stops.campa: Enrolled at the Collège Calvin in the old town, Jorge Luis takes his Latin and his French among Genevan boys who tease him at first for his accent and his foreignness, and who come, within a term, to respect the strange South American who has read more than the masters. He labors over Latin declensions with real difficulty and real devotion; French opens easily, almost by osmosis, from the streets and the classroom both. He will say the city gave him more than any single teacher could have — a whole grammar of Europe entered through a schoolboy's satchel.
stops.quote: A Ginebra le debo la revelación del francés, del latín, del alemán, del expresionismo, de Schopenhauer, de la doctrina de Buddha, del taoísmo, de Conrad, de Lafcadio Hearn y de la nostalgia de Buenos Aires.

stops.name: Geneva, Schopenhauer, Heine, and the Golem
stops.campa: Restless with the school's pace, the boy teaches himself German by the brute method of reading Heine with a dictionary at his elbow, then goes on unaided into Schopenhauer's Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung, a system that will outlast every other philosophy in his private canon. In these same months he comes on Gustav Meyrink's new novel Der Golem, the tale of the clay giant animated by a word hidden in its mouth. Kabbalah enters his imagination here first, as a German expressionist nightmare, years before he meets it again in Madrid as a discipline of hermeneutics and letters.

stops.name: Geneva, the baccalauréat
stops.campa: The Collège Calvin grants him his baccalauréat in the summer, four years and a war after the family meant only to pass a season in the city. Peace has not yet been signed and the borders south are still closed by influenza and troop movements; the family will wait almost a year more before they can leave for the warmer country his father's lungs and eyes both need. Behind him the boy leaves a schoolboy's German and a schoolboy's Latin, and a permanent, lifelong debt to a city he will one day choose, over all others, to die in.

stops.name: Valldemossa and Palma, Mallorca
stops.campa: The family crosses to Barcelona and within weeks to the island, where they pass most of a year between Palma and the hill village of Valldemossa, guests of the Sureda family in their old stone house above the terraces. Here Jorge Luis, not yet twenty, forms a close and lettered friendship with Jacobo Sureda, and the two draft manifestos for a poetic school that exists mostly on paper and in their correspondence. The Mediterranean light after the Genevan winters feels, he will say, like a second and gentler revelation. He writes his first serious verse on this island and burns most of it within the year.
stops.quote: hace unos quince días abandonamos la Ciudad Condal para venir a pasar el verano a las Islas Baleares

stops.name: Seville, "Himno al mar"
stops.campa: On the last day of the year the Sevillian magazine Grecia prints "Himno al mar," dedicated to the poet Adriano del Valle: the first appearance in print of anything Borges has written. He will later call it an attempt, with all his young strength, to be Walt Whitman, and will disown and eventually destroy the little book of "red psalms" it belonged to. But the door is open: in Seville he meets the ultraist poets around the magazine, Isaac del Vando-Villar among them, and hears for the first time the manifesto language of a Spanish avant-garde hungry to break with the past.

stops.name: Madrid, the tertulia of the Café Colonial
stops.campa: In Madrid the family finds Rafael Cansinos-Assens, who presides every Saturday past midnight over a tertulia at the Café Colonial that runs until dawn: poets, translators, unclassifiable men of letters, and at the center this one, who has translated the Thousand and One Nights, the Talmud, and the Zohar into Spanish and speaks of Kabbalah and Sufi poetry with the same unhurried authority he gives to French symbolism. Borges, not yet twenty-one, sits at the edge of the circle and listens. Here, before he has read a line of scholarship on Attar or Ibn Arabi, he first hears their names spoken as living doctrine, not dead footnote.
stops.quote: There the great event to me was my friendship with Rafael Cansinos-Asséns... I still like to think of myself as his disciple.
stops.quote_source: An Autobiographical Essay, The New Yorker, 1970 (written in English)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the return on the Reina Victoria
stops.campa: After a second turn through Mallorca and a last season in Madrid signing ultraist manifestos with Guillermo de Torre and the others of the Colonial, the family sails home. Borges disembarks a convinced avant-gardist, twenty-one years old, carrying in his trunk the beginnings of everything: Whitman's line broken into Spanish free verse, Schopenhauer's pessimism, Cansinos-Assens's Kabbalah, and a case of unpublished poems about a city he has been away from for seven years and now must learn to see for the first time as a grown man, and as a subject for poetry rather than a memory.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the mural magazine Prisma
stops.campa: With a handful of young poets Borges launches Prisma, a single broadsheet of verse meant not for a magazine stand but for a wall: he and his friends go out at night with paste-buckets and glue it to the fences and construction hoardings of Buenos Aires, an ultraism meant to be read standing in the street. He writes his own manifesto for a poetry of the outlying barrios, the arrabal, rather than the fashionable center, and begins the long labor of remaking Buenos Aires — its low houses, its corner stores, its patios — into a mythology equal to the one he has just left behind in Europe.
